title: Peter McCrory on X: 'Why hasn't AI increased unemployment?' — Anthropic's head of economics synthesises 18 months of research into a skill-biased, labor-augmenting framework for why AI has produced no material rise in US unemployment
author: Peter McCrory

dom.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: McCrory accepts that current task-level capability does not imply occupation-level displacement and materially develops the cluster’s account by explaining how incomplete automation, human planning and domain expertise can reorganise jobs around complementary work. He also preserves the cluster’s uncertainty by acknowledging that stronger agents could eventually reduce returns to expertise.
qs: Such empowerment from AI may redraw the boundaries of our roles, and produce new bundlings of tasks within jobs—automating some, reinforcing the importance of others—while on net increasing the marginal product of labor.
It may very well be the case that the skill-biased, labor-augmenting aspect of AI will go away as models continue to improve.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: McCrory accepts the cluster’s core account of jagged, task-level capability and human-led augmentation, then materially extends it with labour-market evidence and an occupational-adaptation mechanism: incomplete automation leaves essential human complements, while jobs reorganise around automated tasks rather than disappearing as fixed bundles.
qs: I'll make a few observations based on work published by the Anthropic Economic Research team, and evidence from the Anthropic Economic Index:  Despite the incredible advance of AI and rapid adoption throughout the economy, there's no job in the O*NET taxonomy (a Department of Labor catalog of occupations and their typical tasks) for which all associated tasks are systematically handled by Claude.

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: McCrory supports the cluster’s qualified conclusion that emerging aggregate productivity gains can coexist with stable employment indicators. His evidence is suggestive rather than causal, and he explicitly acknowledges weaker total factor productivity evidence, reinforcing the synthesis’s caution about interpreting early macroeconomic signals.
qs: I believe we're starting to see AI's impact in aggregate productivity statistics:  Labor productivity growth has been relatively strong in recent years: the ratio of output per hour of work increased 2.0% per year from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1, as compared to 1.6% in the four years prior to the pandemic.
But across quits, layoffs, and job finding rates, we see a pattern of stability.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: McCrory directly supports the proposition that stable unemployment can coexist with adjustment through weaker junior hiring. He distinguishes suggestive hiring evidence from established displacement, stresses causal uncertainty, and argues that current AI use often complements expertise while leaving future displacement and skill effects unresolved.
qs: As Maxim Massenkoff and I documented in our labor impact report, we haven't seen worsening unemployment rates for workers in roles with a large share of tasks that Claude is being used to automate, relative to workers in other roles.
We do find some suggestive evidence that hiring rates for young workers in highly AI-exposed roles have weakened over the past year or so.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: McCrory supports the cluster’s central account of AI as presently reconfiguring and augmenting work rather than causing broad worker replacement. His US labour-market evidence also aligns with the cluster’s conclusion that displacement signals are uneven and concentrated among exposed or younger workers, while causal and longer-term effects remain uncertain. The source is not legal-specific and does not directly address legal apprenticeship or verification risks.
qs: AI (so far) has the hallmarks of a "skill-biased," labor-augmenting technology.
We do find some suggestive evidence that hiring rates for young workers in highly AI-exposed roles have weakened over the past year or so.

kp.k: AI has not materially increased US unemployment, McCrory argues
kp.d: Synthesizing Anthropic's economic research over the past 18 months, McCrory argues that AI has so far had muted unemployment effects, including among workers highly exposed to observed AI automation. This is a cross-domain labor-market argument, not evidence specifically about legal employment. He focuses on the US because of high adoption, economic size, institutions facilitating technological displacement, and rich labor statistics.
qs: In my view, AI has caused no material increase in the unemployment rate to date.

Even if we focus on workers with high exposure to current patterns of AI automation, we don't see unexpected increases in unemployment in recent years (though as I'll discuss below, these workers are more concerned about job loss).

kp.k: Multiple indicators support his assessment of labor-market stability
kp.d: McCrory reports June unemployment of 4.2%, a job-openings-to-unemployed ratio just over 1 in April, and a balanced NY Fed HPW Labor Market Tightness Index. He also cites prime-age employment near multi-decade highs, stably low initial unemployment claims over four years, and layoffs and discharges at or slightly below pre-pandemic levels. These establish his macroeconomic baseline rather than independently identifying AI's causal effect.
qs: The unemployment rate in June was 4.2%, which the Fed views as the level consistent with full employment and stable prices.
Weekly initial claims for unemployment insurance have been stably low over the past four years. And rates of layoffs and discharges remain at or slightly below pre-pandemic levels.

kp.k: AI adoption warrants looking for aggregate economic effects
kp.d: McCrory argues that AI is already sufficiently widespread to produce discernible macroeconomic effects. He reports adoption in at least one business function by approximately 20% of firms and 40% of information-sector firms, with that sector representing 5.5% of GDP. He attributes estimates of quality-adjusted AI output growth exceeding 2,000% annually in both 2024 and 2025 to Patrick McKelvey and his colleague @akorinek.
qs: ~20% of firms use AI in at least one business function. In the information sector, which is 5.5% of GDP, the share is 40%.
Quality-adjusted AI output grew over 2,000% per year in both 2024 and 2025, according to estimates by Patrick McKelvey and my colleague @akorinek.

kp.k: Productivity evidence suggests AI effects but remains mixed
kp.d: McCrory reports labor productivity growth of 2.0% annually from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1, versus 1.6% in the four years before the pandemic, and faster productivity growth in sectors with higher AI adoption. He regards this as suggestive evidence of AI contributions, while acknowledging that more modest total factor productivity growth, particularly after utilization adjustments, weakens the evidence.
qs: the ratio of output per hour of work increased 2.0% per year from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1, as compared to 1.6% in the four years prior to the pandemic.

Total factor productivity growth—how economists like to measure productivity—has been more modest in recent years (especially after accounting for factor utilization). This weakens the evidence, but mixed signals on productivity could themselves indicate that an acceleration is underway.

kp.k: Forward-looking hiring has not produced unusual occupational churn
kp.d: McCrory reasons that firms' expectations about future productivity, wages and employment duration should already influence hiring, separations and occupational switching. Nevertheless, he reports stable quits, layoffs and job-finding rates, no unusually fast AI-related occupational churn, and software engineering job postings broadly rebounding relative to other postings since May 2025.
qs: But across quits, layoffs, and job finding rates, we see a pattern of stability. There's likewise no evidence of unusually fast occupational churn due to AI.

Software Engineering job posts have broadly rebounded since May 2025, compared to all other job posts, indicating rising demand for workers in an occupation where AI capabilities are advancing the most.

kp.k: Young-worker hiring weakness has competing explanations
kp.d: McCrory and Maxim Massenkoff report no relative deterioration in unemployment for occupations with many tasks automated through Claude, including after updating their analysis with newer BLS data. They find suggestive weaker hiring for young workers in highly exposed roles over the past year or so, consistent with Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries in the Coal Mine. McCrory cautions against causal attribution because pandemic adjustments, monetary tightening, commodity shocks, policy uncertainty and remote work may also explain early-career difficulties in a low-hire, low-fire market.
qs: We do find some suggestive evidence that hiring rates for young workers in highly AI-exposed roles have weakened over the past year or so.
But this evidence for young worker displacement should be interpreted with caution.
Right now, young workers may be struggling to find jobs for macroeconomic reasons other than AI.

kp.k: Automation exposure increases anxiety despite unchanged unemployment
kp.d: The reported research distinguishes workers' concerns from realized employment outcomes: workers whose tasks Claude is used to automate express greater concern about job loss, even though the analyses do not yet show unemployment effects.
qs: While we don't see unemployment effects yet, we do find that workers in roles with tasks that Claude is used to automate do express greater concern about losing their jobs than those in less exposed roles.

kp.k: Jagged capabilities preserve returns to expertise and oversight
kp.d: McCrory's central explanatory framework treats current AI as skill-biased and labor-augmenting. Domain expertise, AI proficiency, direction and evaluation complement automation; experts steer systems and recover from failures at uneven capability boundaries. He does not claim that all existing skills retain their value: coding implementation may lose value while delegation and evaluation become more valuable.
qs: So far, AI is both skill-biased and labor-augmenting. It complements domain expertise. It relies on humans in the loop to direct and evaluate the most complex work. And it rewards AI proficiency.
Some types of expertise may become less valuable (e.g. pure coding implementation) even as others become more valuable (e.g. managerial skills of delegation and evaluation).

kp.k: Some occupations remain more vulnerable to outright displacement
kp.d: McCrory identifies technical writers, data entry workers, customer support representatives and computer programmers as occupations where AI can reliably perform core tasks. He reports no unemployment increase for these roles so far, but notes that BLS projections anticipate less growth through 2034 in occupations with higher observed exposure. These projections are distinct from observed displacement.
qs: For instance, technical writers, data entry workers, customer support representatives, and computer programmers are jobs where AI can reliably handle the core set of tasks and responsibilities.
Even though we haven't seen any increase in unemployment for workers in these sorts of roles, occupations with higher observed exposure are projected by the BLS to grow less through 2034.

kp.k: Task automation does not equal whole-job automation
kp.d: McCrory reports that Claude does not systematically handle every associated task in any O*NET occupation. In a fixed-task-bundle framework, essential unautomated tasks constrain total productivity gains and increase returns to human labor. He identifies interpersonal coordination, in-person interactions and physical-world engagement as possible remaining human tasks, while explicitly qualifying that jobs are not actually fixed bundles.
qs: there's no job in the O*NET taxonomy (a Department of Labor catalog of occupations and their typical tasks) for which all associated tasks are systematically handled by Claude.

If jobs are fixed bundles of tasks—they aren't, but more on that in a moment—then the essential, non-automated aspects of work both constrain the overall productivity lift and amplify the returns to labor.

kp.k: Usage research supports complementary expertise and learned proficiency
kp.d: McCrory cites January's Economic Primitives report for a strong correlation between sophisticated inputs and complex outputs, and suggestive evidence that human involvement increases task complexity Claude can handle. He relates difficulties on complex work to METR's reliability–task-horizon tradeoff. March's Learning Curves report finds more successful interactions and greater thought-partner use after six months, which he interprets as evidence that user learning matters.
qs: In our January report, Economic Primitives, we find that sophisticated user inputs and complex Claude outputs are highly correlated.
We find suggestive evidence that humans-in-the-loop increase the complexity of work that Claude handles.

In our March report, Learning Curves, we found that even after just six months of use, people are more likely to interact with Claude as a thought partner, and have more successful interactions with Claude.

kp.k: Expanded scope can reorganize jobs rather than eliminate them
kp.d: McCrory argues that automation can augment labor because technological change reconfigures existing jobs and creates new work combining technical capabilities with human expertise. Among 81k Claude users, expanded scope was a commonly cited source of perceived productivity. He presents new task combinations and higher marginal labor productivity as possible consequences, not established aggregate outcomes.
qs: Widespread task automation can still augment labor. Why? Because jobs are not fixed bundles of tasks.
A commonly cited source of perceived productivity among 81k Claude users was scope—being able to do more, more proficiently.

Such empowerment from AI may redraw the boundaries of our roles, and produce new bundlings of tasks within jobs—automating some, reinforcing the importance of others—while on net increasing the marginal product of labor.

kp.k: Survey respondents anticipate task change more than job loss
kp.d: In June's Cadences Economic Index report, over a third of survey respondents expect AI to perform most or all of their job tasks within twelve months; a similar share expects responsibilities to change for themselves and colleagues. Job-loss expectations are notably lower. More automated Claude use is associated with greater optimism about pay, job security and finding employment; these are respondent expectations rather than realized outcomes.
qs: over a third of all respondents from the Anthropic Economic Index Survey expect AI to be able to do most or all of the tasks they do in their jobs in the next twelve months.
But expectations of job loss were notably lower.
Indeed, those who use Claude in more automated ways tend to be more optimistic about AI's impact on their pay, job security, and ability to find a job.

kp.k: Agentic coding retains complementary human expertise
kp.d: A seven-month analysis of Claude Code usage finds deployment on increasingly valuable tasks alongside persistent returns to expertise. Humans plan and delegate implementation; users with greater domain expertise succeed more often and recover more consistently from model errors. McCrory suggests straightforward coding ability may have lost value while complementary skills gained value.
qs: Claude Code has been used on more and more valuable tasks over the seven months we tracked, but we've seen persistent returns to human expertise: that is, people make planning decisions, and delegate implementation to Claude.
People with more domain expertise succeed in their tasks more often, and recover more consistently when Claude makes an error.

kp.k: Future capability gains could undermine today's augmentation pattern
kp.d: McCrory explicitly leaves open whether more general AI and increasingly autonomous agents will displace labor and reduce returns to human expertise. He speculates that automating innovation, potentially through recursive self-improvement, differs from earlier general-purpose technologies and can generate infinite growth in finite time in otherwise standard economic models. This is a conditional theoretical possibility, not an observed outcome.
qs: It may very well be the case that the skill-biased, labor-augmenting aspect of AI will go away as models continue to improve.
In otherwise standard economic models, automating innovation—which we might see first in recursive self-improvement—can produce economic singularities: infinite growth in finite time.

kp.k: Essential unautomated tasks constrain growth and preserve labor share
kp.d: Drawing on Aghion, Jones, and Jones (2017), McCrory argues that essential tasks left unautomated for technical or societal reasons can prevent economic singularities and sustain labor's income share despite extensive automation. He applies this bottleneck logic to R&D and software production, citing recent evidence that a 10-20x rise in generated code yielded only a 30% increase in software releases and no total increase in app usage.
qs: Such weak links can keep the labor share of income elevated in the long-run, even under very rapid, widespread, but incomplete automation.
Whether AI dramatically accelerates productivity growth requires not just improving capabilities but broad-based automation of tasks involved in the R&D process.
a 10-20x increase in lines of code generated after the introduction of coding agents yielded only a 30% increase in software releases, and no total increase in app usage.

kp.k: Near-term forecast favors productivity growth over higher unemployment
kp.d: McCrory expects substantially better models to accelerate productivity growth and possibly produce clearer signs of recursive self-improvement. Despite his longer-term uncertainty, he predicts that AI will not noticeably raise unemployment over the next year.
qs: I expect this will drive faster productivity growth, and maybe even more clear signs of RSI. But I don't expect unemployment to be noticeably higher a year from now—at least not because of AI.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCrory argues that AI has so far augmented US labor rather than materially increased unemployment, and predicts no noticeable AI-driven unemployment increase over the following year.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of the US economy and AI-assisted work, not a claim specifically about legal services. McCrory describes current AI as skill-biased: it complements domain expertise, requires human direction and evaluation for complex work, and rewards proficiency in using it. He sees suggestive evidence of an aggregate productivity contribution and expects improving models to accelerate productivity growth. He reports no unexpected unemployment increase among highly exposed workers, but acknowledges suggestive evidence of weaker hiring for young workers in exposed roles. Task automation, he argues, can broaden workers' scope and reorganize jobs rather than eliminate them. In agentic coding, implementation may become less valuable while planning, delegation, evaluation and error recovery retain or gain value. He leaves open the possibility that more general and autonomous systems will eventually diminish returns to human expertise and displace labor. Automating innovation could, in economic models, produce extremely rapid growth, but essential tasks that remain unautomated could constrain growth and sustain labor's income share.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: McCrory supports his framework with aggregate labor statistics, exposure comparisons, Anthropic usage research and surveys, and external studies; he explicitly treats several findings as suggestive rather than causal.
pts.d: For labor-market stability, he cites June unemployment of 4.2%, April job openings slightly exceeding unemployed workers, the NY Fed HPW tightness index, high prime-age employment, low initial unemployment claims and layoffs near or below pre-pandemic levels. He reports AI adoption by approximately 20% of firms and 40% in information, and cites McKelvey and Korinek's estimates of quality-adjusted AI output growth exceeding 2,000% annually in 2024 and 2025. For productivity, he reports annual output-per-hour growth of 2.0% from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1 versus 1.6% in the four pre-pandemic years, plus a sectoral association between adoption and productivity growth; more modest total factor productivity growth weakens that evidence. His joint labor-impact report with Maxim Massenkoff, updated using BLS data, finds no relative deterioration in unemployment for occupations with greater observed Claude automation exposure. Weaker young-worker hiring is described as consistent with Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries in the Coal Mine, without quoting an effect size or isolating AI causally. Anthropic evidence includes incomplete task coverage across O*NET occupations; correlations between sophisticated inputs and complex outputs in Economic Primitives; improved interactions after six months in Learning Curves; perceived scope gains among 81,000 Claude users; expectations in the Cadences survey; and seven months of Claude Code usage showing persistent expertise advantages. He invokes METR task-horizon results for reliability limits, economic models for innovation scenarios, and unnamed recent software research reporting much larger code output but limited downstream gains. His one-year unemployment forecast is a judgment based on this synthesis, not a reported forecast-model result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The central conclusion concerns observed effects to date; the explicit unemployment forecast extends one year, while longer-run displacement and innovation scenarios remain conditional.
pts.d: The essay synthesizes the preceding 18 months of Anthropic research and includes productivity data through 2026Q1. It refers to June unemployment and April openings without specifying their years in those passages. Young-worker hiring weakness concerns approximately the preceding year; Claude Code analysis covers seven months; survey respondents anticipate task automation and changed responsibilities within twelve months. BLS occupational growth projections extend through 2034. McCrory cautions that pandemic adjustments, monetary tightening, commodity shocks, policy uncertainty and remote work complicate causal attribution of early-career hiring weakness to AI. Current augmentation depends on uneven model capabilities, incomplete automation, complementary expertise and human oversight. He emphasizes that jobs can change their task composition. Future displacement depends on whether advancing systems overcome those limitations; innovation-led growth depends on broad automation across R&D, not capability gains alone. Essential tasks protected from automation by technical or societal constraints would limit growth and potentially preserve labor's income share.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The effects concern US workers and firms broadly, with uneven implications for young entrants, automation-exposed occupations, experienced domain specialists and software workers.
pts.d: McCrory focuses on the US because of high adoption, economic scale, labor-market institutions and statistical coverage. Highly exposed workers show greater job-loss concern without a corresponding observed unemployment deterioration. Young entrants into exposed occupations may face weaker hiring, though he does not establish AI as its cause. Technical writers, data entry workers, customer support representatives and computer programmers are identified as more vulnerable to outright automation; he reports that more exposed occupations have lower projected growth through 2034. Domain experts and proficient AI users gain from complementary capabilities, broader work scope and more successful interactions. Software workers may see reduced rewards for straightforward implementation but greater rewards for planning, delegation and evaluation. Claude survey respondents anticipate substantial task and responsibility changes more often than job loss, and more automated users report greater optimism about pay, security and employability. These survey results concern respondents rather than the entire workforce. No distinct legal occupation, firm type or legal-market segment is analyzed.
